results.question: Which XLS standard extends XRPL escrow from XRP to issued tokens?
results.conclusion: XLS-85 extends escrow to trust-line tokens and Multi-Purpose Tokens, subject to issuer controls and the TokenEscrow amendment. A specification marked Final is not by itself proof of activation on the network an application uses. Check that network's enabled amendments and the specific token configuration before offering token escrow. [1] [2] The XLS defines AllowTrustLineLocking for trust-line issuers and escrow/transfer permissions for MPT issuances. Authorization and freeze or lock conditions can prevent creation or completion. These constraints mean that adding an issued-currency Amount object to an XRP escrow request is insufficient. The issuer's permissions and the sender's actual token holdings also participate in transaction validity. [1] [2] I recommend a capability check for the complete asset identity, sender, recipient and network before quoting a purchase. Pin the issuer and inspect required permissions. Do not infer RLUSD escrow availability from the existence of an RLUSD trust line or from another token's successful transaction. Read the TokenEscrow documentation and XLS together, then validate against the deployed server's behavior. [1] [2] Exercise disabled issuer locking, missing authorization, frozen holdings and expiry recovery using a testing asset. Record which cases are observed and which are specification-derived. A successful native XRP escrow does not establish success for an issued token. This recommended test matrix follows XLS-85's failure conditions and intentionally avoids asserting a current activation date or claiming that a named stablecoin issuer has enabled every required flag. [1] [2]

results.question: What must a stablecoin issuer enable on its account before holders can lock that issuer's trust line tokens in an escrow?
results.conclusion: XRPL issuers can claw back eligible issued tokens when the required controls are enabled, but native XRP cannot be clawed back. The documentation distinguishes trust-line token controls from MPT issuance flags. Clawback is an issuer capability, not a general right for any dissatisfied buyer to reverse a payment. [1] For trust-line tokens, Allow Clawback must be configured under the documented account restrictions before issuance. The documentation also describes incompatibility with the No Freeze setting. MPTs use an issuance-level capability. These different control surfaces are a reason to inspect the actual asset and issuer rather than treating all fungible tokens as interchangeable. [1] For an agent wallet, I recommend surfacing issuer control risk when selecting a payment asset. Separate a seller refund from an issuer clawback and from expiration-based escrow cancellation. A service should not promise automatic recovery merely because the token standard includes a clawback feature. Whether an issuer can or will act in a particular dispute needs separate legal and operational evidence. [1] Exercise the configured capability on a testing token, a token without it and a native XRP transaction. Record the issuer and issuance configuration used. Do not generalize from those tests to a named stablecoin without examining its real settings. These recommendations derive from the documented controls and intentionally avoid asserting that any issuer has a universal legal entitlement to recover funds in every jurisdiction. [1] For an agent wallet, I recommend allowing only explicitly configured currency-and-issuer pairs. Explain a missing trust line as an asset prerequisite, not evidence that the token is counterfeit. Conversely, creating a trust line should not be described as verifying reserves, guaranteeing redemption or completing customer due diligence. Those are separate questions requiring issuer and operational evidence. [1] An XRPL trust line is a relationship between two accounts for a currency code, used to track trust-line tokens rather than native XRP. A currency code alone does not identify the issuer. Two tokens called USD can represent different counterparties, so a wallet must preserve issuer identity when evaluating balances and payments. [1] The fungible-token documentation distinguishes trust-line tokens from Multi-Purpose Tokens. Trust-line tokens support cross-currency payments and exchange trading, and their rippling behavior can move value between issuers sharing a currency code. Issuer settings and trust-line configuration therefore matter to how a token can be held or transferred. XRP does not become a claim against a token issuer merely because it shares the same ledger. [1] Test identical currency codes from different issuers and reject a quote that changes issuer between discovery and settlement. Inspect rippling and authorization settings before enabling automated routes. Keep token balances separate from XRP needed for fees and reserves. These are design recommendations inferred from the documented token model; they do not establish the creditworthiness of any issuer or authorize buying an asset. [1]

results.question: Which transaction deletes an XRPL account and sweeps its remaining XRP to another account?
results.conclusion: XRPL transaction fees destroy XRP to deter spam, and the required fee can rise with load. The transaction-cost reference gives a standard minimum of 10 drops before load scaling, with separate formulas for multisigning and conditional EscrowFinish. A quoted article price, a token transfer charge and the XRP network fee are different costs; none should be inferred from another. [1] Servers apply a local load threshold and an open-ledger threshold. A transaction can be rejected for an insufficient local fee or queued when it does not meet the current open-ledger cost. Paying a fee is not paying a validator. Conditional EscrowFinish also depends on fulfillment size, so estimating every escrow operation as a plain Payment would understate its requirements. [1] For agent operations, I recommend querying current fee information and applying an explicit maximum before signing. Separate the maximum allowed fee from the amount offered for content. Stop if congestion requires a fee beyond that maximum. Retrying a request should retain the original business intent and reconcile an earlier submission before creating a replacement obligation; fee escalation alone does not establish whether an earlier transaction validated. [1] An informative fee experiment should record the transaction type, offered Fee, validated result and observed network state. Compare uncomplicated Payment, escrow creation and conditional finish without declaring one observation a universal benchmark. Include an insufficient-fee case and an uncertain submission result. These are suggested tests based on the documented fee model; no throughput, future price or completion-time promise follows from them. [1] An XRPL wallet needs a base reserve plus applicable owner reserves, separately from the money it intends to send. The reserve documentation lists Mainnet settings of 1 XRP per account and 0.2 XRP per owned item at access time, and warns that other networks can differ. Validators can change requirements through fee voting; these figures are a dated reference, not a permanent application constant. [1] Base reserve supports the account's existence; owner reserve constrains ledger objects. Escrows, offers and signer lists can affect the latter. Removing an object can release its reserve requirement. Reserves are not payments to validators, and the documentation permits reserved XRP to pay transaction costs. Treating every XRP in a balance as transferable would therefore confuse several distinct accounting concepts. [1] For an agent builder, my recommendation is to estimate spendable XRP from validated account state and the network's reserve settings before authorizing a payment. Include pending object creation in that estimate. A wallet with enough principal for a purchase may still lack room for the escrow object or transaction fee. Report the failed prerequisite precisely rather than silently switching assets or increasing funding authority. [1] Test provisioning with an account near its required reserve, an additional owned object, and removal of that object. Keep the funding source and network in the experiment record. The documentation's special treatment of initial trust lines is another reason to query actual state rather than assume that every account has the same object cost. This is an integration recommendation derived from reserve mechanics, not evidence that a particular deployed wallet passed those cases. [1]

results.question: Which XLS standard defines the native XRPL decentralized identifier ledger entry?
results.conclusion: The fungible-token documentation explains that trust-line tokens can trade and can interact through rippling. XLS-30 adds AMM liquidity that can work alongside order books. An available route is consequently evidence of a possible exchange at particular conditions, not evidence of issuer solvency, off-ledger redemption rights or future market depth. [1] [2] [3] The native XRPL decentralized exchange supports exchanging assets through ledger-based trading mechanisms; it does not guarantee liquidity for every asset pair. Trust-line tokens can participate in exchange and cross-currency payments. Token identity still includes the issuer, so equal currency names do not establish equal economic claims. [1] [2] [3] My recommendation for agents is to quote the exact source asset, destination asset and spending bound before a conversion. Treat conversion as a separate authorized action from buying content. Preserve issuer identity through every route. Inspect the actual delivered amount before fulfilling a downstream purchase, especially where routing or transfer charges mean the amount sent differs from the amount received. [1] [2] [3] Test an empty route, insufficient liquidity and two issuers sharing a currency code. Compare requested bounds with validated balance changes. Do not treat a successful pathfinding response as a completed trade: retain settlement evidence for the executed transaction. These recommendations combine the documented token and AMM models; they do not claim that a particular pair is currently liquid or that using the native exchange resolves compliance requirements. [1] [2] [3] An XLS-40 decentralized identifier identifies a controller and supports verifiable associations, but does not by itself prove a person's legal identity. XRPL's DID documentation explicitly distinguishes a self-created identifier from assertions validated by a trusted credential issuer. An identifier's existence and the truth of claims about its owner require separate evidence. [1] [2] XLS-40 specifies the XRPL DID method and operations for managing DID data. A DID document can supply verification information or refer to externally stored material. The documentation describes resolving a document and checking a credential as distinct steps. A working URI proves neither that an issuer is trustworthy nor that every assertion in the referenced document is current. [1] [2] For an agent marketplace, I recommend keeping controller authentication separate from identity verification and reputation. Verify signatures for the operation being requested, then evaluate issuer policy and credential validity for any identity claim. A seller should not gain a credibility boost merely by creating a DID. Handle broken external references as unavailable evidence rather than automatically substituting a self-description. [1] [2] Test document updates, deleted references and a credential from an issuer the verifier does not trust. Record which public keys and document version were used for verification. Avoid putting sensitive identity evidence in a public ledger simply to make a demonstration easier. These are implementation recommendations grounded in the DID model, not a declaration that a DID constitutes KYC approval or that an identifier owner holds any particular licence. [1] [2]

results.question: Which company created the x402 payment protocol?
results.conclusion: x402 standardizes payment messages and flows for protected resources, while HTTP 402 is a transport signal that payment is required. Its specification separates transport representation from payment schemes and network-specific logic. Receiving a 402 response alone does not prove that a client can pay with an arbitrary asset on an arbitrary ledger. [1] [2] The v2 specification defines payment requirements, a client payment payload and settlement responses, with facilitator interfaces for verification and settlement. Its HTTP transport uses PAYMENT-REQUIRED for requirements and PAYMENT-SIGNATURE for authorization. Scheme and network support must match the requested payment; the protocol's extensibility is not universal implementation compatibility. [1] [2] For an XRPL integration, I recommend documenting the exact supported scheme, network identifier, asset encoding and proof-validation rules. Reconcile the ledger transaction and actual delivery before declaring settlement successful. The partial-payment reference is relevant because requested amounts alone cannot safely establish received value. Keep premium access conditional on the application's verified delivery boundary rather than on an untrusted payment header. [1] [2] Test missing authorization, a malformed payload, the wrong network and a replayed business request. Separate protocol parsing failures from ledger settlement failures in the evidence. These are integration recommendations based on the x402 specification and payment semantics. They do not imply that the upstream specification supplies client budgets, content-quality judgments, escrow refunds or every XRPL-specific scheme used by an application. [1] [2]

results.question: How can an account owner stop the master key from signing so that only a separate agent key can?
results.conclusion: XRPL multi-signing authorizes a transaction when signatures meet the configured signer-list quorum; it does not evaluate the business purpose of that transaction. Signer weights and quorum define which combinations can authorize spending. This separates a ledger authorization rule from the application decision about whether to buy evidence. [1] The multi-signing documentation describes a signer list associated with an account and multiple signatures on a transaction. Multi-signed transactions have a different fee calculation from single-signed transactions. An integration must therefore account for signature count as well as quorum. Installing a signer list is also distinct from deciding which other account authorization paths remain enabled. [1] I recommend separating policy evaluation from key custody: approve a bounded transaction description before asking independent signing components to sign. Those components should verify destination, asset, amount, network and expiration themselves. A second signer that automatically signs anything the first signer proposes provides less operational independence than its existence might suggest. That is a design judgment, not a guarantee made by the ledger. [1] Test insufficient weight, an unauthorized signer, enough valid signatures and recovery after a signer becomes unavailable. Verify account configuration before disabling another signing path so recovery is deliberate. Record whether the test changes key configuration or merely exercises transaction signatures. These suggested checks are derived from quorum authorization; they do not imply that multisigning supplies customer identification, content verification or an application spending budget. [1]
